text: Everything so far in this chapter — the CIS Benchmark, the sysctl settings, the Ansible role enforcing both across a fleet — hardens the host. None of it reaches inside a container, which is really just a Linux process built from an image someone else may have assembled with no hardening in mind at all. A host can score 98% on a CIS scan and still run a container as root, writable, with every default capability, built from an image carrying known CVEs.

Most container images default to running as root inside the container, because that's simplest for the image author. If an attacker ever escapes the container's isolation through a kernel bug or a bad mount, root inside gives them a running start on root outside too. A Dockerfile's USER directive, or an explicit --user flag at runtime, fixes that with almost no cost.

A read-only root filesystem means a compromised process can't write a backdoor or modify the running application in place — legitimate writes go to an explicitly mounted volume instead. Linux capabilities split root's all-or-nothing privilege into dozens of separate grants, and a default container still holds a meaningful subset even without running as root, which is why the CIS Docker Benchmark says drop everything and add back only what's actually needed.

None of that says anything about what's inside the image itself. A base image frozen six months ago can carry published CVEs in its OS packages regardless of how carefully the container runs. Trivy, Grype, and Clair compare an image's installed packages against current CVE databases and can fail a CI build before a vulnerable image ever reaches production.

A fleet with excellent, Ansible-enforced host hardening can still run a container built from an unpatched node:14 image, running as root, writable, with full default capabilities — trivy finds a dozen known CVEs in minutes. The host did its job perfectly; the container undid most of the benefit, which is why it has its own CIS Benchmark. Next up: moving from hardening systems to governing the identities that access them, starting with the joiner-mover-leaver lifecycle.
